Pursuant to the Commission's directions, the Petitioner addressed multiple communications to HPPC dated 5.3.2024, 18.3.2024, 22.3.2024, 26.3.2024, 22.4.2024, 2.5.2024, 8.5.2024 and emails dated 18.5.2024, 22.5.2024, and 4.6.2024, seeking reconciliation of Change in Law claims. Meetings were held between representatives of the parties on 29.3.2024 and 17.5.2024. The Petitioner furnished computation sheets, Auditor's Certificates and other supporting documents as sought by HPPC. Petitioner made oral submissions in support of the prayers in the present Petition. In response, learned counsel for the HPPC submitted that the reconciliation carried out with the Petitioner was provisional in nature, and that the Petitioner has failed to furnish the audited accounts so as to agree to a final reconciliation. After hearing the parties, the Commission admitted the Petition subject to just exceptions and directed the Respondents to file their reply and explain the reason, for non-payment of the admitted amount as per the signed Reconciliation Statement. f) MB Power itself had earlier taken the position in collateral proceedings in Petition No. 356/MP/2022 that the Change in Law Rules are premised on consensus between the parties regarding the nature of the event and its financial impact, and that the Rules do not contemplate a situation requiring adjudication of a disputed claim, thus, MB Power cannot now seek recovery of the disputed amount under the same dispensation. k) As regards the allegation that invoices for February 2023 were not provided, this allegation was raised by HPPC for the first time in its reply and was never raised during the reconciliation process itself. HPPC's conduct of signing the Reconciliation Statement, with full knowledge of the documents provided, amounts to a waiver by conduct or acquiescence, and it is not now open to HPPC to raise objections to the sufficiency of documents on which the Reconciliation Statement was itself founded. In this regard, reliance has been placed on the judgment of the Hon`ble Supreme Court in the case of Kanchan _Udyog Ltd. v. United Spirits Ltd., [(2017) 8 SCC 237_ (Para(s) 22-24)]. 21. During the hearing dated 7.4.2026, the parties made detailed submissions and concluded their respective arguments, and the Commission reserved the Order on the present Petition and the IA. Thereafter, the parties have filed written submissions. 23. After consideration of the submissions of the Petitioner and the Respondents, the following issues arise for our consideration: _“86. In light of the above discussions, Issue No. 2 is decided in favour of the Petitioner, i.e._ **_the Petitioner is entitled to compensation for the shortfall of coal and/or increase in the price of coal on account of the Change in Law._** claimed by the Petitioner as Change in Law compensation, along with Carrying Cost and LPS. 32. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the Respondent, HPPC. The Commission, under Para(s) 86 and 88 of the Order dated 20.1.2024 has categorically held that **_"the Petitioner is entitled to compensation for the shortfall of coal and/or increase in the price of coal on account of the Change in Law”_** and **_“the Petitioner needs to be compensated to the extent of the increase in cost of generation due to the procurement of coal by the Petitioner from other sources in place of coal receipt from SECL at the notified price.”._** (iii) The Petitioner’s claims will be considered once the reconciliation statement is finalised, subject to the outcome of the present Petition. - a) The Order dated 20.1.2024 only directed the parties to reconcile the claims and approach the Commission under Rule 3(8) of the Change in Law Rules and did not direct immediate payment. - b) The Supplementary Invoices raised by the Petitioner have not been verified by the Commission. Further, the methodology for the computation of Change in Law compensation is in dispute in the present Petition. 51. While, HPPC has argued that these Supplementary Invoices are premature in absence of any explicit regulatory direction and the Petitioner’s claims will be considered once the Reconciliation Statement is finalised, subject to the outcome of the present Petition, we fail to understand why HPPC has not reconciled/ signed the Reconciliation 56. We have examined the submissions made by the parties. From the communications exchanges between the parties, it is evident that the Petitioner commenced communications from 5.3.2024 onwards, furnished computation sheets, responded to queries raised by HPPC, participated in the meeting held on 29.3.2024, and supplied the information sought by HPPC on 22.4.2024 and thereafter from time to time. The first Supplementary Invoice was ultimately raised on 13.6.2024, and the reconciliation was finalised only on 25.7.2024, with the delay being substantially attributable to the reconciliation process itself. We, therefore, find no merit in HPPC’s contention that Carrying Cost should be denied for the period preceding the issuance of the first Supplementary Invoice. The Petitioner cannot be deprived of Carrying Cost merely because the reconciliation process, which was to be undertaken jointly in terms of Para 95 of the Order dated 20.1.2024, took time to conclude.
